extracted.intended_audience: young ladies of the United Kingdom (also Wales and the Channel Islands) — readers of a satirical 'text-book' on social types
extracted.subtask_description: A satirical, instructive series of character sketches classifying types of 'young gentlemen' by appearance, manners, typical behaviours in public and private, and advising young ladies how to recognise and respond to them. The piece supplies exemplifying incidents and practical (often ironic) guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bashful Young Gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical and behavioural markers: 'a fresh-coloured young gentleman' with a 'velvet-like, soft-looking countenance', 'crimson blush', and a 'downcast, timid, retiring look'. Typical incidents: convulsive, prolonged handshakes with strangers; hiding behind hangings after awkward introductions; knocking a little girl over; spilling/knocking food (the roll into a tureen of white soup); mixing and misapplying wines; breaking glasses; leaving in another gentleman’s coat and the footman’s hat. Street manner: excessive bowing, dodging, returning and finally shaking hands awkwardly, knocking parcels muddy, banal remarks about the weather or a sister’s health with contradictory replies, then an embarrassed 'Good morning, good morning.' At dances he stands near the entrance, declines the first sets, nervously accepts a partner only to conduct her to a remote corner and fail at conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioural rule-of-thumb for young ladies: recognise the pattern of over-anxiety, physical redness, and awkward social gestures as the bashful type. Remedies: 'bashful young gentlemen should be cured, or avoided.' They are 'never hopeless, and never will be, while female beauty and attractions retain their influence' — i.e., a patient, indulgent woman might 'take a patient in hand' and attempt to 'cure' him; otherwise avoidance is suggested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Out-and-out Young Gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: Appearance and costume markers: rough pilot coat with two gilt hooks and eyes to the velvet collar; buttons 'somewhat larger than crown-pieces'; black or fancy neckerchief loosely tied; wide-brimmed hat with low crown; 'tightish inexpressibles' and iron-shod boots; sometimes carries a large ash stick but keeps hands in pockets; smokes and swears. Social placement: usually employed in a counting-house or solicitor’s office but 'does as little as he possibly can'; frequents streets, taverns, and theatres. Typical public behaviour: walking six or eight abreast to force women into the road, sitting at public venues full-length with hat on (sometimes with knees up if weather dirty), flourishing a stick, crowding and causing a disturbance in passages, squeezing, pushing, whooping; at supper drinking noisily and making a show of beginning to 'spend the evening.' Two sub-classes: those 'who have something to do' and those 'who have nothing' (the latter lack means and rely on companions to fund their pleasures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to identify and respond: treat the out-and-out as raucous, self-asserting, and often inconsiderate—avoid letting 'eccentricity' be a blanket excuse for rudeness. Note family dynamics: if he has mother and sisters, he often treats them with contempt. Social tactic: recognize the out-and-out's 'free-masonry' with similar men (they bond quickly over shared tastes for brandy and noise) and be cautious of their propensity for rowdy behaviour and disregard for women's comfort. Satirical admonition: understand 'eccentricity' in a narrow, Johnsonian sense rather than as a cover for uncivil conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Very Friendly Young Gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: Core trait: extraordinarily affable and attached 'particularly to two, or at most to three families' chosen for dinners or social advantage. Typical behaviours (illustrated by 'Mr. Mincin'): effusive greetings ('I am delighted...very much delighted indeed'), immediate intimacy, profuse smiling and small emotional displays, sharing trivial or distracting news (the pumpkin paragraph), excessive compliments (including praising host’s wife publicly and proposing her at table), performing small services around the house (wheel an easy-chair, close the door, stir the fire), offering medical-sounding remarks about colds, and monopolising conversation by endlessly recounting old jokes and recollections. At larger parties he 'balances his attentions' among many families, carries ladies to supper, helps nervous performers with port wine, and divides his attentions so no elder lady feels neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social reading: the very friendly type is agreeable, useful, and highly social but may dominate attention and conversation; his friendliness is operationally managed (he prioritises families by social returns). For young ladies: welcome the assistance (e.g., calming a nervous singer) but be aware of the performative, sometimes self-serving nature of his affability. The sketch both commends his usefulness and gently satirises the theatricality of his friendliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedicator's Satirical Standards (critique of 'Sketches of Young Ladies')
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefatory critique and meta-guidance: the Dedicator criticises a prior work ('Sketches of Young Ladies' by 'Quiz') as containing 'so many libels' and offences toward 'your Honourable sex' — noting the work classifies women as 'animals' and 'Troglodites', and that the author's assumed name 'Quiz' denotes an intention 'of quizzing.' The Dedicator infers betrayal of confidence (the author must have been trusted by women to obtain his material) and positions his own book as an 'antidote' to the alleged 'bane.' He uses humorous prescription: 'whenever your Honourable sex take twenty-five of Number, 1, you will be pleased to take fifty of Number 2.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production/evaluation norm (satirical): the proper corrective to an insulting or libellous social sketch is to answer with a counter-sketch that exposes men’s follies. Tone guidance: use mock-formality and prescriptive, pill-like metaphors (antidote/bane) as rhetorical devices. Implicit ethical standard: calling entire sexes 'animals' or other injurious epithets is impolite and subject to satirical rebuttal.
